**The Woman at Table Seven**

Elena pressed her nose against the cold glass of the restaurant window, watching the last streaks of amber dissolve into the evening sky. It was a Friday night — traditionally a date night for most — but she had come alone, as she often did these days, to a small Italian bistro tucked into a cobblestoned side street in South London.

She had no date. She had a notebook.

The hostess led her to table seven, a corner spot with a perfect vantage point for people-watching. Elena ordered a glass of Barolo and something rich enough to satisfy the emptiness in her stomach, then opened her notebook and began writing.

It had started six months ago, when she left her job as a community care worker. For three years, she had spent her days visiting the elderly and infirm in their homes — helping them bathe, preparing their meals, sitting with them through the long silences that stretched between television programmes. The work had hollowed her out and filled her up in equal measure. She had learned the significance of small gestures: a hand held during a blood pressure reading, a cup of tea made exactly the way someone's late husband used to make it, the dignity of being asked what you wanted for lunch rather than being told.

One resident, Margaret, had told her: "The human spirit needs more than the basics, love. It needs to be seen."

Elena had carried those words with her ever since.

Now she came to restaurants alone, not out of loneliness but out of a quiet devotion to observation — to seeing people the way Margaret had taught her to. She watched the couple at table three argue in whispers, the woman's fingers shredding a napkin beneath the tablecloth. She watched the man at the bar reading a paperback, entirely content, his nose buried so deep in the pages that his pasta was growing cold. She watched a group of friends erupt in laughter so genuine it made the candles flicker.

She was writing all of it down.

Her notebook was filling with stories — fragments of overheard conversations, sketches of body language, the significance of a lingering glance between strangers. She didn't know yet what it would become. A memoir, perhaps. A novel. Or maybe just a record of what it meant to pay attention in a world that increasingly refused to.

After dinner, Elena stepped outside. She looked up, as she always did, hoping to see stars. But the sky was a flat, muddy orange — the ever-present glow of light pollution washing out the constellations. She remembered reading that satellite observations had confirmed what stargazers had long feared: the nights were getting brighter, and not in a good way. Across the world, artificial light was spreading like a slow flood, drowning out the darkness that had once connected humanity to something vast and unknowable.

Margaret would have hated it. She had once told Elena about lying in a field as a girl during the war, when the blackout regulations turned off every streetlamp, and the Milky Way appeared so vivid it looked like spilled milk across black velvet. "That's when you knew your problems were small," she had said. "When you could see how big everything else was."

Elena tucked her notebook into her bag and began walking home. Her stomach was full. Her heart was full. The sky above was dim and starless, but she carried her own kind of light — the accumulated glow of every person she had cared for, every stranger she had watched, every small moment she had deemed worthy of writing down.

She had no date tonight. But she had not dined alone. She never really did. The world sat with her at every table, if she was willing to look.

And she was always, always looking.
